PySpark Training — Module 2
RDDs
Module-wise plan: 10 modules total, no days or weeks attached. Apply every concept to your own assigned project.
Module 2 — RDDs
Estimated time: 1.5 days full-time. This is a target, not a deadline. RDDs are rarely written directly in modern PySpark,
so this module stays lean: lazy evaluation, partitions, broadcast variables and accumulators matter most.
Two topics, one module: This module combines two topics. Work through Part A and then Part B, each with its own
reference example, guiding questions and done-when list. Both parts are reviewed together in the single PR at the end.
Part A — RDD Basics — Transformations & Actions
Why this matters
RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets) are Spark's original core abstraction, and DataFrames are built on top of them.
Understanding RDDs directly — before the more convenient DataFrame API — is what makes concepts like partitioning and
fault tolerance concrete instead of abstract.
By end of this part, you will be able to
●
●
●
●
Create an RDD from a Python collection and from a file
Apply core transformations: map, filter, flatMap
Apply core actions: collect, count, take, reduce
Explain what 'Resilient' in RDD actually means
Topics to study, in order
●
●
●
●
●
What is an RDD — an immutable, distributed collection of objects, partitioned across the cluster — the R-D-D
name literally describes its 3 defining properties
Creating RDDs — sc.parallelize() from a Python collection, or sc.textFile() from a file — both split the data into
partitions automatically
Core transformations — map (1-to-1), filter (keep matching), flatMap (1-to-many, then flatten) — the building
blocks of almost every RDD pipeline
Core actions — collect (bring everything back to the driver — dangerous on large data), count, take(n), reduce, first
Resilience — how Spark tracks the lineage (the sequence of transformations) of an RDD so it can recompute lost
partitions after a node failure, instead of needing to replicate data everywhere
Hands-on practice
●
●
●
Create an RDD from a Python list of numbers, apply map to square each, filter for evens, and collect the result
Load a text file as an RDD, split each line into words with flatMap, and count total words
Deliberately call .collect() on a large RDD and observe (in the Spark UI or via a simulated large dataset) why this is
dangerous on real cluster-sized data
Reference Example (illustration only — do NOT copy this into your project)
This shows what this topic looks like in a generic reference exercise. Read it to understand the pattern, then design and build
your own version for your assigned domain below.
In the reference exercise, this builds:●
●
●
A script computing word count from a provided text file using only RDD operations (textFile, flatMap, map,
reduceByKey)
A script demonstrating map, filter, and reduce chained together on a numeric dataset, with the final result printed via
an action
A short note explaining why .collect() should almost never be called on a full production-sized RDD
Apply to Your Project — think this through, then build it yourself
Nobody is handing you a spec for these. Think through your own domain's answer to each question, make a decision, and
build it, using your own datasets, columns and logic rather than the reference example's.
●
●
●
Take a log-like or text-like slice of your domain's data (event lines, free-text notes, raw CSV read as lines). Which
single question about it can be answered with map, filter, flatMap and reduceByKey alone?
Implement that question on RDDs and explain what each transformation does to the data.
Which action did you choose to see the result, and why is it safe on large data?
This part is done when
☐ An RDD pipeline answers a real question about your own domain's data, not word count on the reference text
☐ You can explain why you avoided collect on large data and what you used instead
☐ You can explain your design decisions to your mentor: not just that the code runs, but why you built it the way you did
Think About It
Think About It: What does 'Resilient' in RDD actually refer to, and how does lineage tracking let Spark recover from a
lost partition without replicating all your data?
Think About It: Why is .collect() dangerous on a 500 GB RDD but .take(10) is fine?
Part B — RDD Advanced — Persistence, Partitioning & Shared Variables
Why this matters
Once your pipeline reuses an RDD multiple times, or needs data shared efficiently across every executor, naive code
becomes slow or wrong. This module covers the tools that separate a 'working' Spark job from an efficient one.
By end of this part, you will be able to
●
●
●
●
Decide when to cache/persist an RDD and choose an appropriate storage level
Explain what a partition is and why partition count matters for parallelism
Use a broadcast variable to share read-only data efficiently across executors
Use an accumulator to safely aggregate a value across executors
Topics to study, in order
●
●
●
●
●
Caching / persistence — cache() / persist() — telling Spark to keep an RDD's computed data in memory (or disk)
so it isn't recomputed from scratch every time it's reused
Storage levels — MEMORY_ONLY vs MEMORY_AND_DISK vs DISK_ONLY — trade-offs between speed and
reliability when data doesn't fully fit in memory
Partitions — how data is physically split across executors; too few partitions underuses your cluster, too many adds
overhead — repartition() vs coalesce()
Broadcast variables — shipping a read-only lookup value (e.g. a small reference table) to every executor ONCE,
instead of it being re-sent with every task
Accumulators — a write-only-from-executors, read-only-from-driver variable for safely aggregating counts/sums
across a distributed job (e.g. counting malformed rows)Hands-on practice
●
●
●
●
Time an RDD pipeline that reuses the same RDD 3 times, first without caching, then with .cache() — compare
execution time in the Spark UI
Check the default partition count of an RDD you create, then deliberately repartition it and observe the change
Use a broadcast variable to join a large RDD against a small lookup dictionary without a full distributed join
Use an accumulator to count how many rows in a dataset failed a validation check, while processing the data in one
pass
Reference Example (illustration only — do NOT copy this into your project)
This shows what this topic looks like in a generic reference exercise. Read it to understand the pattern, then design and build
your own version for your assigned domain below.
In the reference exercise, this builds:
●
●
●
●
A script demonstrating a measurable speed difference between a cached and non-cached RDD reused 3+ times, with
timings printed
A script using repartition() or coalesce() with a written justification for the partition count chosen
A script using a broadcast variable to enrich a large RDD with a small lookup table
A script using an accumulator to count invalid/malformed records during processing
Apply to Your Project — think this through, then build it yourself
Nobody is handing you a spec for these. Think through your own domain's answer to each question, make a decision, and
build it, using your own datasets, columns and logic rather than the reference example's.
●
●
●
Which small lookup in your domain (a code-to-description map, a rate table) could be shared with every executor as
a broadcast variable?
What would be a realistic 'bad record' in your data (malformed row, impossible value) that an accumulator could
count while you process it?
Which of your RDDs is reused enough to justify caching? Measure it with and without.
This part is done when
☐ A broadcast variable enriches your own data with a domain-specific lookup
☐ An accumulator counts a real category of bad records from your own data, and the count matches a manual check
☐ Your caching decision is backed by timing numbers
☐ You can explain your design decisions to your mentor: not just that the code runs, but why you built it the way you did
Think About It
Think About It: Why does using a broadcast variable for a small lookup table avoid a full shuffle, compared to just
joining two RDDs normally?
Think About It: What would go wrong if you tried to read an accumulator's value from inside a transformation running
on an executor, instead of on the driver after an action?

daily commits while working and no need to push yet. Commit Part A's work and Part B's work separately, so your
mentor can see the two halves distinctly in review. Once the ENTIRE module is complete, push the branch and open one
PR to main, assign the mentor as reviewer, and merge after approval. Then branch off the updated main for the next
